---
title: Tables
description: How one item holds many small records as rows in typed columns, and why a row is not an item.
job: A builder learns how an item holds rows in typed columns and why a row is not an item.
kind: concept
---

Some things are many small records under one heading: the bottles in a wine cellar, the lines of a budget, the messages of a conversation. Making each an item would bury the item list, so **one item holds them as the rows of a table**, and stays one thing to find, tag, link and move to the bin.

## Where a table comes from

**A type declares the tables its items hold,** each with named, typed columns: `core.conversation` declares a `messages` table. **A `core.table` item chooses its own columns,** in its `columns` property, for a table kept by hand, such as a reading log.

A column has a type, such as `string`, `integer`, `date`, `enum` or `item`, which holds another item's ID. It can be required, can say how it **adds up**, such as `sum` or `count`, and can be **searchable**. The contract's [tables](https://github.com/withmarfa/marfa/blob/main/conformance/spec/tables.md) chapter has the limits.

## A row is not an item

A row is its `id`, its `values` keyed by column, and when it last changed. **It has no version, tags, edges or history of its own.** It belongs to its item: a key reads and writes its rows as it may read and write the item's type, and an item in the bin takes its rows with it. Writing rows leaves the item's `version` alone and moves its `last_activity_at`.

## Write rows in batches

Every write is a **batch**: a list of operations on one table of one item, applied in order, **all or none.** `put` creates a row or replaces the whole row its `id` names, `patch` sets the columns it names, and `delete` removes a row.

A row has no version to compare, so **a `put` replaces every column**: to change some columns, `patch` them. When two writers patch the same column, the later write wins. Send an `Idempotency-Key` with a batch you may retry, so a repeat is answered, not written twice. This adds two wines to a table whose `bottles` column adds up, and reads the total:

<Terminal>

```bash
marfa rows put 01a1fc3d-d23c-71c5-876c-0959f5a1e4c1 table --values '{"wine":"Chablis","vintage":2021,"bottles":3}'
marfa rows put 01a1fc3d-d23c-71c5-876c-0959f5a1e4c1 table --values '{"wine":"Barolo","vintage":2018,"bottles":8}'
marfa rows totals 01a1fc3d-d23c-71c5-876c-0959f5a1e4c1 table
```

```text
created row 01a1fc3d-d9c0-75c8-9a57-fb4a71c8da7c in table as batch 01a1fc3d-d9c0-75c8-9a57-fb49d3f24bcf
created row 01a1fc3d-e0ec-77c3-aa10-596d0afd8ca8 in table as batch 01a1fc3d-e0ec-77c3-aa10-596c031600b8
row_count           2
totals.bottles.sum  11
```

</Terminal>

A `core.table` item's one table is named `table`.

## Take a batch back

Each table keeps a **change log:** every batch that changed a row, with each row as it stood before. **Undoing a batch puts those rows back,** as a new batch, so undoing the undo redoes it. An undo is refused with `undo_conflict` when a later batch has changed one of its rows to a third state. `marfa rows undo` takes one back.

## Read and follow rows

**A read can filter and sort by any column,** and totals answer how many rows a filter selects and what each adding-up column comes to. The server can keep a large table's order by a column it's sorted by, so deep pages stay fast. An `item` column sorts as no value, so its pages come in `id` order. **Search matches rows as well as items.**

**A batch that changes rows sends one `rows.changed` event,** so an app that follows the [event stream](/build/events) keeps its rows current.
